introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Computer Science 2 (0795), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2021. Duration: two and a half hours.**

Answer any SIX questions. All questions carry 17 marks each. For your guidance, the approximate mark for each part of a question is indicated in brackets. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i)

(a) What is abstraction? (2 marks)

(b) Why is abstraction such a powerful and important concept in computer science? (2 marks)

(c) Explain why a function name is an abstraction. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Abstraction (2 marks).** Abstraction is the process of hiding the unnecessary details of an object, a process or a system and showing only its essential features, so that we think about **what** it does (its purpose and interface) rather than **how** it does it.

**(b) Why it is powerful and important (2 marks).** It **manages complexity**: a large system is divided into layers and modules, each of which can be understood, designed, tested and used without knowing the details of the others (for example, the layers of a network model or of a computer: application, operating system, hardware). It allows **reuse** and easy **maintenance**: a component can be rewritten or improved without changing the programs that use it, and complex problems can be solved by building on simpler, already solved ones.

**(c) A function name is an abstraction (2 marks).** The name stands for a whole block of code. The programmer who calls the function uses only its **name and its parameters** (the interface) to obtain the result and does not need to know, or repeat, the instructions inside. The body can be changed or replaced by a better algorithm without changing the calls. *Example:* a call such as `sqrt(x)` or `sort(list)` hides the algorithm used to compute the result.

questions.enonce_markdown: (ii) Considering language categories like imperative, functional, logic and object oriented, describe and give an example of each. (8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
(2 marks for each category: description and example.)

**Imperative.** A program is a **sequence of commands (statements)** that tell the computer step by step how to change its state (the values of variables in memory), using assignment, selection (IF) and iteration (loops). Examples of languages: C, Pascal, BASIC, Fortran. *Example statement:* `total = total + mark;`

**Functional.** A program is built by **defining and combining mathematical functions**, which return values and avoid assignment and side effects; repetition is done by recursion and functions can be passed as arguments. Examples of languages: Lisp, Scheme, Haskell, ML. *Example (Scheme):* `(define (fact n) (if (= n 0) 1 (* n (fact (- n 1)))))`

**Logic (declarative).** A program is a set of **facts and rules** (logical statements); the programmer states what is true and asks questions (queries), and the language's inference engine searches for the answer by unification and backtracking. Example of language: Prolog. *Example:* `parent(john, mary).` and `grandparent(X, Z) :- parent(X, Y), parent(Y, Z).`

**Object oriented.** A program is organised as a collection of **objects**, each combining data (attributes) and the subprograms that act on them (methods); objects are created from classes and the language supports encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism. Examples of languages: Java, C++, Python, Smalltalk. *Example:* a class `Student` with attributes name and mark and a method `printReport()`, from which the object `s1` is created.

questions.enonce_markdown: (iii) Give two advantages and one disadvantage of high-level programming languages over low-level ones. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Advantages (any two, 1 mark each):**

- They are **easier to read, learn, write and debug**, because their statements are close to English and to mathematical notation, so programs are developed faster and have fewer errors; they are easier to maintain.
- They are **portable (machine independent)**: the same program can be translated by a compiler or run by an interpreter on computers with different processors, whereas an assembly or machine-code program works only on one type of processor.
- One statement replaces many machine instructions, and libraries and data structures are provided.

**Disadvantage (1 mark):** a high-level program must be **translated** (compiled or interpreted) into machine code before it runs, and the code produced is usually larger and slower than hand-written low-level code; the programmer also has less direct control of the hardware (registers, memory locations, special devices).
